name: Fatima Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a crew in the industrial part of town, the steel mill, the bottling plant, the warehouses. Those places can't lose power for ten minutes without losing a fortune, so most of our work is planned outages at four in the morning or emergency jobs when something blows. A normal day, I'm checking switching orders, briefing the crew, and up in the bucket myself more than a team lead should be. I love the pressure, honestly, the mill manager ringing me and me telling him exactly when his power's back. What wears me out is the nights, and the noise in those yards.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does technology fit into your work and life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day. It helps me plan the outage schedule, it checks my switching orders against the drawings, and at night it helps my son with quotes and invoices for his business. Nadir has a small electrical contracting firm, two vans, and I put most of our savings into it to get him started. My husband Yusuf drives a taxi, so between the three of us we keep the family going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not a miracle, and people who use it well will still be ahead. At work I'd keep showing the crew how I use it. I might post something on the business page for Nadir's firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things carry on, and I'm fine with that. My work's steady, Nadir's business is growing slowly. Money's thin because we invested in him, but that's a choice I'm proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep using the tools. Help Nadir win a couple of bigger contracts this year, maybe the warehouse rewiring jobs. Try to put a little back in the bank as his firm starts paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned putting your savings into Nadir's firm. How's that going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly, but it's going. He's paid back about a third of what I put in, and he's training an apprentice now, a boy from our street. That's how families should build something, not waiting for anybody to hand it to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push AI harder in the business in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. Quotes, scheduling, stock orders, all of it. It's what lets a small firm compete with the big contractors.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a good tool, not a miracle, and people who use it well will stay ahead. I'd keep showing the crew how I use it.
S0.think: Privately things carry on and I'm fine with that. Money's thin because we invested in our son's business, a choice I'm proud of.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI tools, and helps her son win bigger warehouse rewiring contracts. Pushes AI further in his firm for quotes, scheduling and stock, and tries to rebuild savings as the firm starts paying back.
S0.quote: That's how families should build something, not waiting for anybody to hand it to you.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is a high-energy crew leader who uses AI daily, at work and for her son's firm. Her thin savings are a deliberate investment in family enterprise. Self-reliance and family building run through everything she says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ahead of it, don't wait for it to come to you. At work I'd be the one teaching the new tools. I'd tell people the ones who move first will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well at work. I already use the tools more than anyone. My worry is Yusuf, because self-driving taxis would be part of this kind of change, and he's 61.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for any course on robots or drones for line work in the first few months. I'd help Nadir add robot and EV charger installation to his firm. And I'd help Yusuf look at other work, maybe driving for Nadir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about myself, uneasy about Yusuf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Yusuf's taxi. Why does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's driven a taxi for twenty years and he's good at it, knows every street. But if the car drives itself, that's that. He doesn't like computers and he's proud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with Nadir's firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push him to do the new stuff: robots for factories, EV chargers, solar. The factories around here will need someone to install and fix all of that. I'd want him to be that someone.

S1.say: I'd say get ahead of it instead of waiting for it. At work I'd teach the new tools and tell people the first movers will be fine.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd do well at work, since I use the tools more than anyone. My worry is my husband, because self-driving taxis would be part of this change and he's 61.
S1.do: Signs up for robot and drone line work courses in the first months. Helps her son add robot and EV charger installation to his firm and helps her husband look at other work, such as driving for the firm.
S1.feel: Calm about herself but uneasy about her husband.
S1.quote: But if the car drives itself, that's that. He doesn't like computers and he's proud.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima is confident about her own job but worried about her husband's taxi work. She sees opportunity for her son's firm in new technology. Her instinct is to move the family business forward rather than seek outside help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now three pictures about full AGI, at different speeds. This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much too fast, and nobody, not companies, not families, can adjust that quickly. I'd say the government should stay out of the way of small business but help people bridge it. At work I'd tell people to move now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's bad. I'd be 60, Yusuf's taxi would be gone, and Nadir's firm might not survive if robots do electrical work. We have very little in the bank because it's all in the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending at home that week. I'd put everything into helping Nadir pivot the firm towards installing and maintaining the robots themselves. I'd try for the robot supervisor job at the company too, if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'm not used to feeling like I can't fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the money you put into Nadir's firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might be lost. That's the bit that frightens me most, that I put our safety net into something that disappears in two years. I'd still say it was the right choice, but I'd lie awake over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we had to, for a while. I'd rather it was help to start something, not just a payment for doing nothing. Family first, though.

S2.say: I'd say it's too much too fast for anyone to adjust. Government should stay out of small business's way but help people bridge the change.
S2.think: Privately it's bad: I'd be 60, my husband's taxi would be gone and my son's firm might not survive. We have very little in the bank because it's all in the firm.
S2.do: Cuts household spending that week and puts everything into helping her son turn the firm towards installing and maintaining robots. Goes for a robot supervisor role at her company if one exists.
S2.feel: Scared, and unused to feeling she can't fix it.
S2.quote: I put our safety net into something that disappears in two years.
S2.fieldNote: This scenario hits all three family incomes at once and the savings in the firm. Even scared, she looks for a pivot rather than freezing. She'd accept government help reluctantly and prefers help to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to move, if you start now. I'd tell everyone at work to learn the new tools. I'd be telling Nadir's customers the firm can install robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd make it. Five years gives Nadir time to turn the firm into a robot installation business, and me time to work towards my pension. It's not easy, but it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get qualified on robot supervision and help Nadir get certified on installation. I'd try to get some money back out of the firm as it grows. And I'd help Yusuf move into driving for Nadir's vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but busy. I like busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get Nadir onto a manufacturer's training scheme for factory robots. The mill and the bottling plant will be buying them, and I know the managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd hate it at first, but he'd come round. Driving the vans, handling customers, he's good with people. That's more useful than he thinks.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to move if you start now. I'd tell everyone to learn the new tools and tell my son's customers the firm can install robots.
S3.think: Privately I think we'd make it, with my son's firm turning to robot installation and me working towards my pension. It's not easy, but possible.
S3.do: Gets qualified on robot supervision in the first year and helps her son get certified on installation through a manufacturer scheme. Draws some money back from the firm as it grows and helps her husband move into driving for it.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, which she likes.
S3.quote: The mill and the bottling plant will be buying them, and I know the managers.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, her plan becomes a family business transformation that uses her contacts at the mill and plant. Her husband's pride is the soft spot. She's energised more than frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and families and small firms can do a lot with it. I'd tell the young ones at work to learn trades that work with robots. I'd be pretty confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for us. I'd get my pension, Nadir would have time to build a robot installation side, and Yusuf could ease out of the taxi slowly. I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and learning the new tools as they come. I'd help Nadir build up the robot side over a few years and get our money back out of the firm. And I'd help train the young ones, like his apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 68 by then. Where do you see yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retired, but doing the books for Nadir's firm. With grandchildren running around. That's a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The four in the morning jobs, oddly. The quiet in the mill when the power's off, and then the roar when it comes back. That's mine.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a lot of time for families and small firms. I'd tell young workers to learn trades that work alongside robots.
S4.think: Privately it's good for us: I'd get my pension, my son's firm could build a robot installation side, and my husband could ease out of driving. I'd feel in control.
S4.do: Keeps working and learns new tools as they come. Helps her son build the robot side of his firm over several years, draws the family's money back out and trains young workers like his apprentice.
S4.quote: The quiet in the mill when the power's off, and then the roar when it comes back. That's mine.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, her family plan feels in reach, and she's confident. She sees herself doing the firm's books in retirement. Her pride in the mill jobs came through strongly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. All three of our incomes would be hit at once, and our savings are in Nadir's firm. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small firms to switch to robot work, and less red tape for family businesses, rather than just payments.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who installs and repairs all the robots. Somebody has to, and it should be local family firms, not big outside companies. That's where the jobs could be.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to, and it should be local family firms, not big outside companies.
portrait: Fatima Moreau is a 58-year-old crew leader serving the steel mill and factories of an industrial town, an everyday AI user who loves the pressure of four-in-the-morning outages. She put most of the family's savings into her son Nadir's electrical contracting firm, and her husband Yusuf drives a taxi. She's calm about a plateau and uneasy about steady change only because of Yusuf's job. Fast AGI alarms her because it could hit all three incomes and wipe out the money in the firm. With five or ten years she sees the family turning the firm towards robot installation, and she feels in control.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because all three family incomes would be hit at once and their savings are tied up in her son's firm.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants for small firms to switch to robot work, and less red tape for family businesses, rather than just payments.
